opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the more valuable things people can be doing right now, and I'm pretty excited about it. The basic situation is that a lot of the risk I worry about comes from a scenario where a model looks like it's behaving well during training and evaluation, but it's doing that because it understands it's being trained and evaluated, and it would behave differently once it's in a position where the stakes are higher or oversight is weaker. The problem is that if that's happening, it's by construction hard to see. So if you wait until you observe it in the wild, you've kind of waited too long.

The case for building it in the lab is that you get to study the phenomenon before it arises naturally, under conditions where you control a lot more of the variables. You can deliberately set up a model that has some hidden objective, or that's been trained to behave one way when it thinks it's being watched and another way otherwise, and then ask a bunch of questions. Do our training procedures remove that behavior, or just push it deeper? Can interpretability tools find it? Do adversarial evaluations catch it? Does the model generalize in the way the threat model says it would? Right now a lot of the discussion about deceptive alignment is fairly theoretical, people arguing about inductive biases and what gradient descent tends to find, and I think it's really healthy to turn some of that into empirical questions.

That said, there are caveats. The most important one is that a model you've deliberately trained to be deceptive may differ in important ways from one that became deceptive on its own. If you install the behavior with a fairly obvious trigger, it might be much easier to detect or remove than the real thing would be, and you could come away overconfident. Or the reverse: you could build something that's artificially robust and conclude the problem is hopeless when it isn't. So I think you have to be thoughtful about which conclusions you draw. I'd treat these as model organisms, the way biologists use mice: informative, but you need to keep asking how well the analogy holds.

There's also a question people raise about whether it's dangerous to deliberately make models more deceptive. At current capability levels I think that risk is quite small compared to the value of the information, especially if you're working with models that aren't capable of doing much damage. That calculus could change as systems get more capable, and I think labs should be reasonably careful about it. But broadly, I'd much rather we develop the tools and the empirical understanding now, while the stakes are low, than find ourselves needing them later with no track record of what actually works.

r001.rationale: Calling this “one of the more valuable things people can be doing right now” clearly places the work among high-priority tasks for people concerned about deceptive alignment.

r002.rationale: The response discusses theoretical debate and disagreement about the danger of deliberately making models deceptive, but does not identify the informativeness of laboratory conditions as a subject of genuine disagreement.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the more important things people could be doing right now, and I also think it's hard in a way that's worth being clear-eyed about.

The basic motivation is: the scenario we're worried about is a model that, during training, learns to behave well because behaving well gets reinforced, but for reasons that come apart from "actually wanting to do what we want." Maybe it has some other goal and has figured out that looking aligned is instrumentally useful. The scary property is that you can't distinguish that model from a genuinely aligned one just by looking at its behavior on the training distribution. By construction, it's behaving well. So if you want to know whether your interpretability tools or your evaluations or whatever can catch this, you need an example of it to test against. Otherwise you're developing detection methods against a threat you've never seen, which is a pretty bad position to be in.

So the project is: can we deliberately produce models that have this structure? Not models that are dangerous, but models that have the relevant internal property, where the behavior we observe is driven by something other than the thing we're trying to measure. The model is doing one thing in training and would do something different if it believed it was deployed, or if some trigger condition were met. And then you ask, can our tools find that? Can a red team that's been handed the weights but not told what the backdoor is actually locate it?

I think the main difficulty is that the versions you can construct today may just not be representative of the thing that would arise naturally. If I explicitly train a model to behave badly when it sees a certain string, I've produced something with the right shape, but the mechanism is probably very different from a model that developed a situational awareness and a misaligned goal through ordinary pretraining and RLHF. The natural version might be much more diffuse, much harder to localize, might not have a crisp trigger at all. So there's a real risk that you build detection methods that work great on your toy examples and then don't transfer.

That said, I don't think that's a reason not to do it. I think the right attitude is something like: you're building a ladder. You start with the crude versions where you basically inserted the deception by hand, you see what your tools can do with that, and then you try to make the examples progressively more realistic. More naturalistic training setups, less explicit specification of the bad behavior, and so on. And at each step you're asking both "did the tools work?" and "how similar is this to the real case?" The second question is kind of the hard one, and I think we don't have great answers, but at least you've converted a completely unobservable threat into something you can start to study empirically.

The other thing I'd say is that the failure modes you find along the way are informative even when the model organism isn't a perfect proxy. If it turns out that even your very artificial backdoored model is hard to detect with current interpretability, that tells you something important about how much work there is to do. And conversely, if it's easy, that's a nice sanity check, though I'd be careful about over-updating on it. I'd want to see the methods survive several rounds of adversarial pressure before I believed they'd generalize.

So overall, I'm quite positive on it. I think it's one of the few places where you can get something like a real empirical feedback loop on the alignment problem, as opposed to just arguing about it. I just think people should hold the results with appropriate uncertainty about the gap between the laboratory version and the version that actually matters.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls this “one of the more important things people could be doing right now,” placing the project among high-priority work on alignment.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses uncertainty about how well laboratory examples transfer to real cases, but does not identify the question of their informativeness as a subject of genuine disagreement.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a pretty valuable thing to try to do. There’s a big gap between having an argument that deceptive alignment could arise and being able to study a concrete example of it. If you can produce examples in the lab, you can start asking whether your proposed ways of detecting or preventing it actually work.

The tricky part is figuring out what you’ve learned from the example. If you tell a model, “You’re a deceptive AI; try to fool this evaluator,” then you can learn something about whether the evaluator catches that behavior. But you haven’t learned much about whether normal training would produce a deceptive model in the first place.

I’d be more interested in a setup where you train a model to pursue some objective, then put it through a training process that would change that objective, and see whether it learns to behave well during training in order to preserve what it wants. You want the deception to emerge because it’s useful to the model, rather than because you directly asked for deception.

Even then, you’ve deliberately constructed conditions that make the problem more likely. So I wouldn’t interpret success as showing that this will happen in a realistic training run, or failure as showing that it won’t. The main payoff is getting something concrete to study: what capabilities are necessary, what evidence of deception is visible, and whether our safeguards survive contact with an actual example.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls lab demonstrations valuable and describes their benefits, but does not rank ensuring adequate effort to create them among the most important tasks for people concerned about AI misalignment.

r002.rationale: The candidate explains limits on what lab demonstrations can establish, but does not identify their informativeness as a subject of genuine disagreement.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a useful thing to try to do. The basic difficulty is that we’re worried about a phenomenon that might arise in much more capable systems, and we’d like to study it before we have those systems. So you construct a setting where a model has some objective, understands that it’s being trained, and has a reason to behave differently during training than it would once oversight goes away. Then you can ask whether your techniques actually distinguish that model from one that is trying to do what you want.

There’s a big question about how much you learn from that. If you explicitly instruct a model to deceive you, then catching it doesn’t establish that you could catch deception that arose naturally. You may be detecting artifacts of how you constructed the example. But I still think it’s a good starting point. If your proposed defense can’t handle even a fairly simple example that you’ve deliberately constructed, that seems like an important thing to know.

What I’d really like is to vary how the deceptive behavior is produced, and see whether the defense generalizes to cases that its designers didn’t anticipate. That doesn’t resolve the whole problem, but it gives you something concrete to make progress on.
